source.title: Repetition Mismatch: Why Data Mixture Experiments Don't Scale and How to Fix Them
source.authors: Kevin S. Zhou; Lisa Alazraki; Kris Cao; Marek Rei

record.tranche_reason: The study experimentally tests whether small-budget runs predict larger-budget outcomes, but for optimal data-mixture proportions rather than the claim versions’ loss laws or parameter/token allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper measures held-out validation loss to choose and compare data mixtures, and reports errors in predicting target-horizon mixture proportions. These results concern mixture extrapolation, not power-law loss scaling, parameter/token compute-optimal allocation, architectural sensitivity, other modalities, or downstream predictability. Rows are recorded as related findings with versions ["none"]. The paper also discusses scaling-law literature and cites findings from other work; cited results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study does not test the claim. It predicts optimal data-mixture proportions across training horizons at fixed model size, using a linear-regression baseline it calls 'scaling laws' plus repetition-matched subsampling. It fits no power law of loss in parameters, tokens or compute, and it does not extrapolate loss, optimise the parameter/token split, vary shape at fixed size, or measure downstream tasks. Kaplan and Hoffmann are only cited as assuming abundant data. The record's 'tests'/T2 is wrong.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that repetition mismatch is a primary reason small-scale mixture experiments fail to transfer. Matching the target repetition rate lets one cheap horizon (about 6% of target tokens) recover near-optimal mixtures at 124M–1.17B. The benefit grows with model capacity, with a lower bound at 30M where the method fails. The paraphrase should add that repetition should be treated as a first-class variable in mixture optimisation.
record.recipe_differences: The study does not reproduce either original scaling-law method. It compares linear extrapolation of optimal data-mixture proportions across horizons with a document-level subsampling procedure that matches the high-quality data's repetition rate.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with repetition-control method, high-quality dataset, model size, number of mixture sources, and number of training horizons. The 30M models are an exception where one-horizon repetition control performs worse; at 1.17B the multi-horizon linear baseline can overtake repetition control after three or four horizons.

fits_no_version.finding: Two-source results (Table 1): one-horizon repeat-aware prediction error is 0.05–0.15 at 757M–1.17B versus 0.65–0.85 without repetition control. At 30M repetition control is worse (0.55 vs 0.25). At 1.17B the linear baseline overtakes it at 3–4 horizons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Matching the target repetition rate of scarce high-quality data improves prediction of the target-horizon optimal mixture from short runs. The benefit depends on model size and number of horizons.

fits_no_version.finding: Three-source results (Table 2/11): at 757M, two repeat-aware horizons recover the optimum (2.7699). At 124M, the four-horizon prediction gives 2.91950 vs the 2.91820 optimum. A single horizon leaves a loss gap of about 0.08–0.10.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Repetition-controlled short runs can predict multi-source mixtures, but more horizons are needed as the mixture space grows and as model size shrinks.

fits_no_version.finding: Optimal repetition count of the high-quality data at the target horizon is model-size dependent: about 5 at 757M/1.17B and about 24 at 30M (Figure 1, Figure 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The repetition threshold beyond which repeated data gives diminishing returns depends on model size.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: Models are at most 1.17B parameters and target horizons are approximately 3.8B tokens. Most configurations use single runs; the authors report a three-seed check for five PubMed configurations per method and bootstrap intervals for 1.17B target-horizon mixture sweeps. Evaluation is limited to held-out high-quality-domain loss, not downstream tasks or full-corpus objectives. The selected rows concern data-mixture prediction, not the claim versions' scaling-law quantities.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1's 4-H results for 30M, 124M, and 345M; 2-H and 3-H results for other model/source combinations; Table 1's remaining 2-H and 3-H results; Tables 7–10 and 12–15's detailed three-source subsample sweeps; Table 11's other three-source tuned mixtures and baselines; and the bootstrap and multi-seed per-configuration loss results in Tables 6 and 16 are not individually extracted. The rows retain the central one-horizon comparisons, selected multi-horizon cases where outcomes differ, and highlighted three-source predictions and target optima.

untested.parts: No power-law fit of loss vs parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolates optimal mixture ratios by linear regression, not loss via fitted power laws.
Model size is fixed per experiment; no compute-optimal N/D allocation.
Depth and width are scaled together to change size; no fixed-parameter shape comparison.
Repeated high-quality data is studied only for its effect on the mixture optimum; no power-law form is fitted for repeated data or other modalities.
No downstream tasks are evaluated; the authors say so explicitly.
No loss-law exponents or N/D split are fitted, so their dependence on setup or fitting choices is not examined.

record.verdict_notes: The paper's 'scaling laws' label refers to linear extrapolation of optimal mixing ratios across horizons, not a power-law loss fit, so its rows cannot bear on V1–V7. The reader's relation and tranche (tests/T2) are corrected to discusses/T6. All row versions stay ['none']. Models are 30M–1.17B parameters with about 3.8B-token horizons, mostly single runs.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law relationship between held-out loss and parameter count, training tokens, or compute is fitted or tested.
The study predicts target mixture proportions, not the held-out loss of larger runs from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Model size is held fixed within each mixture-prediction experiment; the study does not optimize parameter and token counts at fixed compute.
Architecture depth and width are varied to obtain different model sizes, but architecture effects at fixed parameter count are not tested.
The experiments use English text pretraining; other modalities, repeated-data scaling laws as such, fine-tuning, and transfer are not tested.
No downstream task performance or relationship between downstream performance and pretraining loss is measured.

The study shows that repetition affects data-mixture prediction, but it does not test the claim’s fitted loss-law exponents, compute-optimal parameter/token split, or curvature away from a single loss power law.
